Q: Ingress not adding the application URL for Grafana dashboard A:

Your ingress rule is correct, and nginx creates the correct virtual host to forward traffic to Grafana's service (I left only the needed strings to show it):

 server {
    server_name sample.com;
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    set $proxy_upstream_name "-";

    location ~* ^/grafana/(?<baseuri>.*) {

        set $proxy_upstream_name "default-grafana-grafana-80";

        set $namespace      "default";
        set $ingress_name   "grafana-ingress-v1";


    rewrite /grafana/(.*) /$1 break;
    rewrite /grafana/ / break;
    proxy_pass http://default-grafana-grafana-80;

    }

And yes, when you go to sample.com/grafana/, you get the response from the Grafana pod, but it redirects to the sample.com/login page (you see this from the screenshot you provided):

$ curl -v -L http://sample.com/grafana/
*   Trying 192.168.99.100...
* Connected to sample.com (192.168.99.100) port 80 (#0)
> GET /grafana/ HTTP/1.1
> Host: sample.com
> User-Agent: curl/7.47.0
> Accept: */*
>
< HTTP/1.1 302 Found
< Server: nginx/1.13.5
< Date: Tue, 30 Jan 2018 21:55:21 GMT
< Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
< Content-Length: 29
< Connection: keep-alive
< Location: /login
< Set-Cookie: grafana_sess=c07ab2399d82fef4; Path=/; HttpOnly
< Set-Cookie: redirect_to=%252F; Path=/
<
* Ignoring the response-body
* Connection #0 to host sample.com left intact
* Issue another request to this URL: 'http://sample.com/login'
* Found bundle for host sample.com: 0x563ff9bf7f20 [can pipeline]
* Re-using existing connection! (#0) with host sample.com
* Connected to sample.com (192.168.99.100) port 80 (#0)
> GET /login HTTP/1.1
> Host: sample.com
> User-Agent: curl/7.47.0
> Accept: */*
>
< HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
< Server: nginx/1.13.5
< Date: Tue, 30 Jan 2018 21:55:21 GMT
< Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
< Content-Length: 21
< Connection: keep-alive
<
* Connection #0 to host sample.com left intact
default backend 404

Because, by default, Grafana's root_url is just /:

root_url = %(protocol)s://%(domain)s:%(http_port)s/

and when the request redirects to just sample.com, nginx forwards it to default backend 404.

Solution:

You need to change root_url in Grafana's server setting to /grafana/:

root_url = %(protocol)s://%(domain)s:%(http_port)s/grafana/

You can do this changing this setting in Grafana's configmap object.

Q: A valid exception to "Never touch managed resources in the finalizer"? A:

I am not worried about thread safety. I am worried about ensuring that the buffer is returned to the pool just once but not until after all threads are done with it.

If I were to put a using statement in front of my retrieval of the CameraImage object, then I would be forced to create a copy of it (or at least of its ArrayPool buffer) whenever I wanted to hand it off to another thread. That is what I ended up doing.

What I hoped I could do (in my example above) was to not have a using statement and not have to make a copy to hand it off to another thread but rather rely on the finalizer to call the Dispose function and return it to the pool once the GC decided it was time. This approach would have allowed me to not have to worry about calling Dispose.

Unfortunately, that approach is not safe because, as you pointed out, ArrayPool has no guarantee to hold on to the buffers you rent from it while they are rented. Which means the GC could conceivably collect that buffer before my Finalizer ran. Then my finalizer would call Dispose and try to return a buffer to the pool when it had already been GC-ed. That would be bad.

Cloning the buffer is the simplest solution for me. I only hand the buffers off to other threads intermittently. Not every time I grab one. And the threads to which they are handed off are clearly defined. So I can ensure that each one Disposes of its own copy.

Mostly I was hoping to find a way to make this allocation much more GC efficient while simultaneously bulletproofing it against future developers who might not know the protocol. It was not to be.

declare -f gpm will just print the function definition of function gpm with no other text.

Q: When to use pointer to a class and when to just instantiate it as a variable A:

It's just to make it look good. Basically classed as 'syntactic sugar' for readability and to make your code a bit more presentable so to cover it:

ptr->foo() 
//is literally 
(*ptr).foo()

The meaning of making pointers to classes is that if you have different child classes you can access them through it (though I don't really know anything so take that with a lot of salt). But dereferencing it like this:

*ptr.foo()

would access foo and then try to dereference it which wouldn't really work in this case. So you dereference ptr first then access foo.
